walkthroughs.body_html:
Population & Migration — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Population & Migration brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Population & Migration.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Roughly what % of Japan's population is over 65?
What does a wide-based pyramid show?
options: Ageing population
Youthful population
Decline
Stability

mcqs.q: What is the difference between push and pull factors in migration?
options: Push factors are physical and pull factors are economic.
Push factors drive people away from their origin (war, poverty, persecution, disaster); pull factors attract people to a destination (jobs, safety, family, healthcare, education).
Both birth and death rates fall sharply in Stage 2.
Push and pull factors are the same thing.

mcqs.q: Why do people move from rural to urban areas in LICs?
options: A combination of push factors (rural poverty, lack of services, agricultural change) and pull factors (perceived jobs, education, healthcare) — though reality often disappoints.
Because cities in poor countries are always better than the countryside.
Because the government forces them to move to cities.
Both birth and death rates fall sharply in Stage 2.

mcqs.q: What happens in Stage 2 of the Demographic Transition Model?
options: Death rates fall rapidly (due to better food, sanitation and medicine) while birth rates remain high, causing rapid population growth.
Both birth and death rates fall sharply in Stage 2.
Because the government forces them to move to cities.
Birth rates rise rapidly because people want larger families.
